newsitem.title: CHINA: HK under pressure to deport hundreds of children.
newsitem.headline: HK under pressure to deport hundreds of children.

text.p: Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa came under pressure on Saturday to combat a feared huge influx of children sneaking across closely-guarded borders from the Chinese mainland.
The issue, involving divided families, creates a major dilemma for Tung's post-colonial government in the first week of rule as a Special Region of China.
Smugglers of human cargoes paid by relatives run a thriving trade spiriting children over the border, eluding police checks.
Hundreds of youngsters risk their lives to rejoin a parent here, hustled covertly into Hong Kong by boat or truck by "snakehead" smugglers.
An estimated 60,000 children from "split families" are waiting to settle in the territory.
Hong Kong's police chief went to the south China city of Shenzhen on Saturday to discuss tighter frontier controls.

The Hong Kong government will ask law-makers next Wednesday to empower an immediate repatriation of hundreds of illegal child migrants from the Chinese mainland, the Hong Kong Economic Times reported.

Chief Executive Tung's office was not immediately available for comment on the report. The independent Chinese-language newspaper said the government would ask the China-appointed interim assembly to rush through the law so the government could expel young Chinese illegals here without proof of identity.
Police chief Eddie Hui vowed to stop illegal migrants trying to enter crowded Hong Kong, which cannot cope with tens of thousands of mainland illegal children flooding in.
Hui left for talks with Chinese officials in the frontier city of Shenzhen. "We will make sure the illegals do not pass through the border," he said.

On Friday, hundreds of families flocked to Hong Kong's immigration headquarters to surrender illegal immigrant children smuggled in from China, hoping to be allowed to stay after Beijing took over the territory from the British on Tuesday.
"I think we should have some firm policies and firm actions instead of just saying we are concerned," said Allen Lee, a Hong Kong lawmaker.
The independent Hong Kong Economic Journal said the government, which began life on July 1, was ill-prepared with the seriousness of the problem.
"If the Special Administrative Region government does not take any measures at once, we believe a large influx of illegal child migrants (from China) will begin," it said.

The rush to surrender the youngsters was sparked by an announcement on Thursday that "child illegals" could remain here while their parents' background was checked to determine if they had a right to stay.
Most of them were fathered by Hong Kong men and born to mainland Chinese women. Both the mother and the children have to apply for residency rights to join their husbands in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's new constitution says mainland-born offspring of a Hong Kong permanent resident are entitled to stay here.

But under current arrangements, their application to Chinese authorities for permission to migrate to Hong Kong can take years as only 150 Chinese immigrants, about 66 of them children, are allowed into the territory each day.
Although Hong Kong reverted to China earlier this week, border control between the two place remains intact.
